cards.title: Exponential lower bounds for deciding rKt complexity
cards.formal: Historical question, answered affirmatively for exact decision: does deciding randomized time-bounded Kolmogorov complexity require exponential time even for randomized algorithms? Fix a standard efficiently universal randomized Turing machine U, define rKt_U(x) below, and let L_U={(x,1ˢ): rKt_U(x)≤s}. Hirahara’s Theorem 5.3 establishes that there is a constant ε>0 such that L_U∉BPTIME(2^{εN}), where N is the encoded input length and ε may depend on the fixed machine conventions. Thus no uniform randomized algorithm within that worst-case time bound decides every input correctly with probability at least 2/3. The source’s broader question has an exponential lower-bound answer; stronger variants that allow arbitrary behavior inside a promise gap must be distinguished.
cards.why: Establishes unconditional exponential computational hardness for recognizing a concrete measure of information content, even when the deciding algorithm can use randomness.
cards.status_note: Matched the general 2019 exponential-hardness question to Hirahara’s published CCC 2022 Theorem 5.3 for exact decision. Read the machine definition, threshold encoding and the gap theorem’s qualification, and checked the February 2026 follow-up. Resolution is recorded for exact decision; no claim is made that the stronger promise-algorithm variant or the 2019 fixed probability-gap formulation has thereby been settled. No independent proof audit.

progress.text: Oliveira proves quasipolynomial randomized-time hardness and asks for an exponential lower bound.
CCC Theorem 5.3 proves exponential hardness of exact rKt threshold decision. The stronger gap theorem has an explicit all-input bounded-error caveat.

cards.definitions: The fixed universal machine U takes a binary program d, an auxiliary string y, and a tape of independent uniformly random bits. It simulates encoded machines with polynomial overhead; the machine and program encoding are fixed independently of every input. For λ∈(0,1], rKt_{U,λ}(x|y) is the minimum of |d|+⌈log₂t⌉ over finite binary programs d and integers t≥1 such that U(d,y) outputs exactly x and halts within t steps with probability at least λ. Failure to halt in time counts as failure. The probability is over the first t random tape bits, which suffice for a t-step computation. No advice, oracle or input x is supplied to the decoding machine. Write rKt_U(x)=rKt_{U,2/3}(x|empty string). The decision input gives x explicitly and a nonnegative integer s in unary, separated by a fixed delimiter; its length N=|x|+s+O(1). The unary convention avoids hiding a very large time threshold in a short integer. BPTIME(T(N)) consists of languages decided by one uniform randomized Turing machine that halts within O(T(N)) steps on every input and random tape, and has error at most 1/3 on every input. The ε lower bound is an existential constant-rate exclusion; it is not a claim that every input requires exponential time. Standard machine and encoding choices change constants. The exact threshold language has no promise gap. In the later logarithmic-gap variant, yes-instances satisfy rKt_U(x)≤s and no-instances satisfy rKt_U(x)>s+C log₂|x| for a sufficiently large fixed C; the intermediate range is outside the correctness promise. In the 2019 source another variant instead separates descriptions succeeding with probabilities β and α, using β=3/4, α=2/3 and threshold |x|/2 in its default notation. These variants must not be identified solely because they are all called MrKtP.
cards.answer_criterion: An unconditional exclusion L_U∉BPTIME(2^{εN}) for some ε>0 settles the exact-decision exponential-lower-bound question. This is the published 2022 Theorem 5.3. Lower bounds on the number of bits needed to describe some strings, or hardness under an unproved assumption, would not by themselves establish it. The separate stronger claim against every promise-respecting randomized gap tester is not certified as solved here.

context_blocks.title: The 2019 baseline was much weaker
context_blocks.text: The source proves hardness beyond randomized quasipolynomial time for rKt decision and approximation variants, then asks for an exponential lower bound. Its description-length-plus-log-time measure accounts for random decoding.

context_blocks.title: The exact threshold question has a published answer
context_blocks.text: Hirahara defines the total unary-threshold language in Section 5 and proves its constant-rate exponential randomized time lower bound as Theorem 5.3. The introduction explicitly compares the new exponential scale with Oliveira’s previous quasipolynomial result.

context_blocks.title: A crucial limitation of the gap theorem
context_blocks.text: Theorems 1.4 and 5.8 additionally rule out infinitely-often fast bounded-error language algorithms consistent with the logarithmic-gap promises. Such an algorithm must have a bounded-error acceptance decision on every input, including the intermediate gap. The paper explicitly distinguishes this from a general promise algorithm, which may have acceptance probability near 1/2 inside the gap.

context_blocks.title: Recent work preserves that distinction
context_blocks.text: The February 2026 preprint explains why Hirahara’s BPTIME lower bound cannot replace a prBPTIME lower bound in its application. It also gives a different theorem for conditional rKt with a potentially longer auxiliary string; that is not a resolution of the remaining unconditional gap-tester variant.

cards.context:
The source proves hardness beyond randomized quasipolynomial time for rKt decision and approximation variants, then asks for an exponential lower bound. Its description-length-plus-log-time measure accounts for random decoding.

Hirahara defines the total unary-threshold language in Section 5 and proves its constant-rate exponential randomized time lower bound as Theorem 5.3. The introduction explicitly compares the new exponential scale with Oliveira’s previous quasipolynomial result.

Theorems 1.4 and 5.8 additionally rule out infinitely-often fast bounded-error language algorithms consistent with the logarithmic-gap promises. Such an algorithm must have a bounded-error acceptance decision on every input, including the intermediate gap. The paper explicitly distinguishes this from a general promise algorithm, which may have acceptance probability near 1/2 inside the gap.

The February 2026 preprint explains why Hirahara’s BPTIME lower bound cannot replace a prBPTIME lower bound in its application. It also gives a different theorem for conditional rKt with a potentially longer auxiliary string; that is not a resolution of the remaining unconditional gap-tester variant.

meta.status_scope: No claim of exhaustive open-status verification
methodology: Detailed cards have individually written statements, context, significance, and documented results. Source notes are unfinished research records and do not yet meet that standard. The legacy index is retained for traceability.
Open in the source means open at the date of that source. The build date, 10 September 2026, does not establish current open status. Old excerpts may omit conditions or subsequent results.

Selection considers model power, necessary resources, sharp bounds, structural characterizations, explicit constructions, and minimal assumptions. Source notes use a heuristic screen; detailed cards give an individual explanation.

The earlier automatic paper screen allowed at most one new card per paper title and rejected identical formulations and close duplicates within a source. Approved textbook and survey imports retain multiple distinct questions per publication. Confirmed overlaps supplement existing cards; collection-wide semantic deduplication remains incomplete.

Short quotations retain the source language. Later related literature, where listed, is a research aid rather than evidence of resolution. Personal notes and saved cards are stored locally in your browser.

Textbook and survey questions are dated paraphrases; source locations, conjectures, research directions and caveats are preserved on the problem cards. These annotations do not establish current open status or change a later card review. New source drafts remain unassessed for importance. The reader contains the imported questions and external bibliographic references only; source files are not bundled.

Selection groups follow the agreed 10 large and 25 small categories. We aim for benchmarks of 100 and 500 problems, with a possible expansion to 1,000. All three use the same category order and the same ranking within each category. The respective prefixes are 5/2, 25/10 and 50/20 problems per large/small category. The possible 1,000-problem expansion has 1000 assigned places and 0 reserved places. Each card records its category explicitly. These counts describe saved candidates; classification does not verify a statement or its current open status. Deleted records are absent from the catalogue and exports. Their stable IDs and reasons are retained to prevent reimport. Final quota selection and a comprehensive deduplication audit remain pending.

Importance ordering is an editorial assessment of foundational significance, breadth of consequences, and influence on other questions. Each assessed card gives a reason. The category-wide review also uses shared priority bands for questions of comparable scope; it does not claim that these ties have a scientifically meaningful internal order. Unassessed drafts share a provisional score of 50; their relative order is only an ID tie-break, not an importance judgment. The first 5/2 places in each large/small category are an explicit editorial focus selection balancing importance and topical diversity. Focus ordering does not alter importance scores; remaining candidates use score and ID order. The targets are 100 and 500 problems, with a possible expansion to 1,000. Top 100, Top 500 and the possible Top 1000 use the first 5/2, 25/10 and 50/20 category places respectively, all from the same ranking. Category positions include all candidates and remain fixed when filtering. Publication date, source date, and card detail do not increase importance. Records marked resolved are placed after the remaining candidates, without changing their historical importance score. Importance review does not establish that a saved question is still open.

benchmark_selection.basis: Individual editorial review of saved titles, importance rationales, problem statements, source notes and working summaries. This is a review of importance and topical diversity, not a fresh verification of open status or completion of draft formulations. Importance scores are preserved.
